title: Why tech outages could be the new normal for months across the US
html:
“It’s going to be bumpy for the next six months,” said former National Security Agency hacker David Kennedy, now CEO of the cybersecurity firm TrustedSec, to The Post.

“I’ve never seen so many service outages in a week’s span in my entire life.”

Some cyber experts fear that America’s recent tech problems may be setting up a future larger issue. AFP via Getty Images

Many of the recent significant service failures such as the Nov. 13 historic FAA ground stoppage and massive issues with Microsoft and several large banks have been attributed to tech glitches, including some involving changeovers related to AI, as opposed to hacking.

While NYU Tandon School of Engineering professor Justin Cappos acknowledged that the “Microsoft and the FAA outages were absolutely abnormal events,” he said many of the other issues that followed were related to faults in recent automation and not targeted attacks.

Advertisement

“If you’re going to be doing things like integrating AI into systems and laying off people, then you do need to be very concerned about what impact this is going to have,” he said.

Tech outages could continue for months, experts warn. NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock

Some experts are not convinced that the other big snafus were not hack-related, though.

Advertisement

“The combination of timing, the volume, the companies, and the industry verticals that were in play is definitely very suspicious to me,” Kennedy said, noting that the targets “are very much what an adversary would go after.”

It is “absolutely possible” that the recent glitches — also including a cyber hit on Europe’s major gas supplier, Equinor — are the result of an intelligence assessment by a foreign state as preparation to launch a future, more significant attack, he said.

Lisa Palmer, the CEO of AI firm Neurocollective.Ai, said she has a similar gut instinct over the recent pattern.

“In many cases, you’ve got AI-powered humans that are on offense, and you have traditional software-powered humans that are playing defense,” she said.

Advertisement

“I particularly worry about certain government agencies that are underfunded – and that includes local and state government agencies as well.”

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy (right) speaks alongside FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford after the Nov. 13 air ground stop. AFP via Getty Images

If the recent outages do have a state culprit, “Iran is a potential, but I would put my eggs in the basket around China,” Kennedy said.

“China is very methodical. They don’t think in a two-year, four-year political cycle. They think 20 years, 30 years, 40 years ahead,” he said, speculating that the nation would want to disable US infrastructure in the event of invading Taiwan.

“They’ve been hacking our grid for 20 years. We’ve been booting them out for 20 years.”

Cyber experts agree that tech layoffs have played a role in the ongoing outages. Bird Photographer TH – stock.adobe.com

The experts say substantial tech sector layoffs in favor of artificial automation – Microsoft alone cut 9,000 jobs in 2025 – have also led to bad actors using AI to rapidly exploit system weaknesses no longer in human hands.

“I’ve been a hacker for 25 years, and [AI] hacks better than I can,” Kennedy said. “It’s creating a lot of chaos in the enterprise right now.”

“Corporations are looking at AI for cost savings, and that’s not realistic in cybersecurity right now.”

J.S. Nelson, a University of Pittsburgh law professor who specializes in cybersecurity, thinks the two schools of thought aren’t mutually exclusive.

“These problems with our automated systems could have multiple sources,” she said, blaming “at least three categories.”

Advertisement

“Foreign state or criminal actors exploiting vulnerabilities, companies rushing to fix vulnerabilities ahead of — or in the wake of — such potential attacks, and use of AI that creates new problems as the systems start to act in unexpected ways.”

Regardless of the potential causes, dramatic lifestyle changes and extreme doomsday prepping are ill-advised.

“I think we’re going to be able to handle it. I don’t think it’s going to be catastrophic or the end of human civilization or the United States or things like that,” Kennedy said.
summary: “In many cases, you’ve got AI-powered humans that are on offense, and you have traditional software-powered humans that are playing defense.”
